---
title: "6.9 Zero Inflated Count Models"
---

- The negative binomial model produces higher Pr(*y* = 0) compared to the Poisson model due to the overdispersion parameter
- But, Poisson and negative binomial can struggle with DVs that are ≈ ≥ 50% zeroes because they assume every observation has a positive probability of \> 0
  - E.g., Everyone has a non-zero chance of drinking alcohol; of having at least one depressive symptom; of smoking a cigarette; etc.
- In zero inflated models we assume:
  - Zeroes can occur by multiple processes:
    - Some people **always have 0 counts**; some **might have 0 counts**
    - This leads to a greater proportion of 0s since they occur two ways
      - We say "the zeros are inflated"
  - Positive counts (i.e., \> 0) are generated by one process just like Poisson or negative binomial
- Zero-inflated models can be motivated theoretically (interested in both the zero or not process as well as the count process) or by necessity of a DV with high proportion of zeroes

## The with zeros model: didactically useful

- Zeroes occur through two processes
  - **Group A**: People who **always** have 0 counts
  - **Group S**: People who **sometimes** have 0s, but **sometimes not**
- Probabilities of being in each group

$$\begin{aligned} \Pr(\text{Group A}) &= \psi \\ \Pr(\text{Group S}) &= 1 - \psi \end{aligned}$$

- An observed 0 could come from either group; we don't observe directly in the data whether someone is in Group A or S
  - This is discrete, unobserved heterogeneity
- Probabilities of counts by group

$$\text{Group A:} \quad \Pr(y = 0\,|\,\mathbf{x}) = 1$$

$$\text{Group S:} \quad \Pr(y\,|\,\mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{y}}{y!} \quad \text{where } \mu = \exp(\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol{\beta})$$

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
i.e., Group S's counts are produced by a Poisson process
:::

$$\text{Group S:} \quad \Pr(y = 0\,|\,\mathbf{x}) = \exp(-\mu)$$

## Zero inflated models

### Step 1: Model group membership as a binary model

- First, we model the probability of group membership: whether a person is in A(lways) zero or S(ometimes) zero:

$$\Pr(\text{Group A}\,|\,\mathbf{x}_{i}) = \Pr(\text{Always zero}\,|\,\mathbf{x}_{i}) = \psi_{i}$$

  - Where the probability $\psi$ (psi) can be modeled with binary logit or probit
- Remember we don't directly observe if someone is in group A or S
  - Therefore, we use what is in the data for our best guess
    - Specifically, we observe whether someone is observed as a zero or not on the DV along with their values of theoretically important IVs
    - That is, which variables in the data do we think would predict group A vs S membership?
      - Include them in the binary model
- For the next step, we actually use the probability of **not** always being a zero ($1 - \psi$)

$$\Pr(\text{Always zero}\,|\,\mathbf{x}_{i}) = \psi_{i}$$

$$\Pr(\text{Not always zero}\,|\,\mathbf{x}_{i}) = 1 - \psi_{i} = \Pr(\text{Sometimes zero})$$

### Step 2: Model counts by weighting by Pr(Group S)

- Next, we predict the counts but only for people with observed counts
  - That is, we do not include observed zeroes in this step
- However, some people who were observed with \>0 counts are sometimes zero so would not always have counts (e.g., we asked them about \# of drinks last month right after the holidays)
  - Therefore, take the Pr(sometimes zero) into account when predicting counts
- The predictions in zero-inflated models are effectively weighted by the probability of *not being an always zero*
  - For those we generally think are always zeros (Pr(Always) = 1; Pr(Sometimes) = 0), we give them almost no weight in the calculations of the counts
  - For those who are very unlikely to be an always a zero (i.e., usually have a non-zero count), we give the most weight
    - E.g., Whose Pr(Always) approaches 0; Pr(Sometimes) approaches 1
- For ***Zero Inflated Poisson***:

$$\Pr(y\,|\,\mathbf{x}) = (1 - \psi)\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{y}}{y!} \quad \text{for } y > 0$$

- For ***Zero Inflated Negative Binomial***:

$$\Pr(y\,|\,\mathbf{x}) = (1 - \psi)\frac{\Gamma(y + \alpha^{-1})}{y!\,\Gamma(\alpha^{-1})}\left(\frac{\alpha^{-1}}{\alpha^{-1} + \mu}\right)^{\alpha^{-1}}\left(\frac{\mu}{\alpha^{-1} + \mu}\right)^{y} \quad \text{for } y > 0$$

## Example: Days in last month of "not good" mental health

- GSS (2002, 2006, 2010, 2014)
- DV: *"Now thinking about your mental health, which includes stress, depression, and problems with emotions, for how many days during the past 30 days was your mental health **not good**?"*
  - Happily (get it?) this measure has an excess of zeroes
    - ≈ 60% of the sample reports zero days of 'not good' mental health
- IVs: Gender, income, age, marital status
- Controls: Race, education, religiosity, survey year

## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss", clear
(cda_gss.dta |  GSS 1972-2021 CDA - Categorical Data Analysis | date created 202
> 3)

. keep if year >= 2002 & year <= 2014
(50,180 observations deleted)

. 
. *Data management
. gen notrelig = relig
(106 missing values generated)

. lab var notrelig "R Not Religious"

. recode notrelig 1 2 11 = 0 4 = 1 3 5/10 12/13 = .
(18,560 changes made to notrelig)

. lab def notrlab 0"Christian" 1"Not Religious"

. lab val notrelig notrlab

. 
. drop if missing(mntlhlth, physhlth, woman, race3, year, college, ///
>     parent, faminc, metro, notrelig, married)
(13,623 observations deleted)

. 
. *6.9.a
. hist mntlhlth, percent fcolor(none) ///
>     title("[6.9.a] Distribution of 'Not Good' Mental Health Days in Last Month
> ")
(bin=37, start=0, width=.81081081)

```

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(dplyr)           # data manipulation
library(ggplot2)         # graphs
library(cleanplots)      # graph scheme
cleanplots_defaults()

gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta")
gss <- gss |> filter(year >= 2002 & year <= 2014)

# Data management: Christian (Protestant, Catholic, Christian) vs not religious
gss <- gss |>
  mutate(notrelig = case_when(relig %in% c(1, 2, 11) ~ 0, relig == 4 ~ 1))

gss <- gss[complete.cases(gss[c("mntlhlth", "physhlth", "woman", "race3", "year",
  "college", "parent", "faminc", "metro", "notrelig", "married")]), ]

# 6.9.a
ggplot(gss, aes(x = mntlhlth)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(100 * count / sum(count))), binwidth = 1,
    fill = NA, color = "black") +
  labs(title = "[6.9.a] Distribution of 'Not Good' Mental Health Days in Last Month",
    x = "days of poor mental health past 30 days", y = "Percent")
```
